title: The hypertrophy series: the optimal measure of progression for muscle growth
summary: NH says the best way to judge hypertrophy progress is performance: rising strength and ever-increasing tonnage, not body measurements, which move too slowly. Past the novice technical peak, and outside specialized strength programs, strength gains reliably reflect muscle gain, but strength must stay a means, not the goal.
claims: Body measurements are the worst way to judge progress in the gym
The best measure of hypertrophy progress is performance: strength progression feeding ever-increasing tonnage
Absolute strength numbers do not matter for bodybuilders; what matters is that they keep growing
Arm measurements grow so slowly that tracking them either discourages you or misleads your programming
Neural strength gains mostly affect novices, who still gain muscle; after a technical peak, strength gains reflect muscle growth
Specialized frequency-manipulation strength programs can raise one lift without much muscle, but he never prescribes them
Strength moves much faster than size: a biceps goes from about 10 to 22 inches while a curl can go from 40 to 140 lb, and total tonnage by tens of thousands of pounds
Strength progress fuels the drive for results but must never become the goal itself
Progressive overload is his method for driving performance
